title: MTD From April 2028: What the £20,000 Threshold Means
excerpt: The MTD qualifying-income threshold is scheduled to fall again for April 2028. If your relevant income is above £20,000, that later start date may affect your planning. It does not mean everyone earning £20,000 must use MTD today.
metaTitle: MTD £20,000 Threshold: Planning for April 2028 | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check the scheduled April 2028 MTD £20,000 threshold against 2026/27 gross qualifying income and distinguish later preparation from an existing obligation.
featuredImageAlt: A smaller trader plans future record-keeping with a long-term calendar and labelled-by-colour yearly folders.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

content:
The MTD qualifying-income threshold is scheduled to fall again for April 2028. If your relevant income is above £20,000, that later start date may affect your planning. It does not mean everyone earning £20,000 must use MTD today.

Match the threshold to the income year

HMRC's current timetable brings in people with qualifying income over £50,000 for April 2026, over £30,000 for April 2027 and over £20,000 for April 2028. The corresponding tax returns and income years matter when establishing an individual's start date.

For the April 2028 stage, check qualifying income for 2026/27. Qualifying income concerns gross self-employment and property income, rather than the profit left after expenses. Salary is not simply added to that turnover figure.

Do not confuse turnover and take-home pay

A sole trader with substantial expenses might have profit below £20,000 while gross business income exceeds it. A landlord can similarly have rent above the threshold even after finance costs and other spending leave a much smaller cash surplus.

Give your accountant the gross figures for each relevant source and explain any jointly owned property, ceased activity or newly started business. Those details can affect the assessment.

What you can do before the start date

Keep business records consistently and retain statements from platforms or letting agents. Establish who will maintain digital records, which software will be used and who will send updates and prepare the annual return.

You do not have to treat every later-cohort enquiry as an immediate subscription purchase. Confirm the actual start year and decide whether earlier preparation or voluntary participation would be useful.

Recheck before acting

This article reflects the timetable checked on 20 October 2026. Future legislation, guidance or your circumstances can change, so review the position before the relevant tax year begins.

TaxSimba can discuss accountant-led support for the service period you need. Start with the eligibility question, then agree a suitable start date and scope rather than assuming that the date of an online enquiry is the date quarterly obligations begin.

Put it into practice

A future threshold uses a specific income year

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A sole trader expects £17,000 gross trading receipts and £5,000 gross property income for 2026/27. The relevant combined figure is £22,000 before expenses, so she checks the scheduled April 2028 start rules and any applicable exception. She does not subtract mortgage payments or use salary in the total. She also checks whether an earlier year's figures already required MTD, rather than assuming the later £20,000 stage delays an existing obligation.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Which income year supports the 2028 start?Check 2026/27 qualifying income under the published timetable.
Are the figures gross and complete?Combine relevant trading and property sources using the correct joint share.
Does an earlier obligation already apply?Review earlier waves and current circumstances before choosing a service start date.

Two more questions you may have

Does earning £20,000 mean everyone must join MTD today?

No. The scheduled threshold, look-back year, income type and individual circumstances all matter.

Should I subscribe years early just because of the headline?

Confirm the actual start date first. Preparation and voluntary participation are separate choices to assess against your needs.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Record gross 2026/27 qualifying sources.
  • Document joint-income shares.
  • Check earlier MTD start rules.
  • Plan software and regular record keeping.
  • Recheck official rules before the relevant start year.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Is a Receipt Photo Enough for MTD? What Your Records Need
excerpt: A photograph of a receipt can support an expense, but it is not automatically the complete digital transaction record required for MTD. The image and the accounting entry do different jobs.
metaTitle: Receipt Photos and MTD: Complete the Digital Record | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Receipt photos support MTD records but do not replace transaction entries. Check extracted dates, amounts, categories, business purpose and duplicate imports.
featuredImageAlt: A trader places a receipt photo beside a structured ledger entry, both evidence and record visibly distinct.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Create digital records - Guidance
GOV.UK — Business records if you're self-employed: Overview

content:
A photograph of a receipt can support an expense, but it is not automatically the complete digital transaction record required for MTD. The image and the accounting entry do different jobs.

What the transaction record contains

HMRC's guidance requires digital information about the amount, date and appropriate category of income or expense. The detail depends on your business and whether a permitted simplification applies. The record must be created and stored using software within the MTD process.

A picture sitting in your phone gallery does not, by itself, establish that the expense has reached the accounting records. If receipt software extracts the details, someone still needs to check that the amount, date and category are correct.

Keep the reason for the spending

A receipt can show what was purchased without explaining why it was for the business. Add context for unusual items and identify personal use. Ordinary clothing or a private meal does not become deductible because it has been photographed.

For example, a receipt for a tool used partly at home may require a business-use adjustment. The image is useful evidence, while the accountant decides how the allowable amount should be reflected in the records.

Prevent duplicate expenses

The same cost might appear in a bank feed and in a receipt upload. Those should usually be matched rather than treated as two purchases. Tell your accountant if you submit the same document through more than one route or replace an unclear image.

Keep supporting documents legible, complete and accessible. Store them with enough detail to reconnect them to the accounting entry later; a cropped image without the date or supplier can be difficult to use.

Agree a simple handover routine

Ask how your accountant wants documents supplied and how they will tell you about missing information. Providing records regularly gives time to resolve questions before quarterly deadlines.

TaxSimba's accountant-led service uses the information you provide to maintain the agreed records. Uploading evidence starts that process; review, correct recording and the separate submission outcome still matter before an MTD update is treated as complete.

Put it into practice

One receipt, one properly matched transaction

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A business owner photographs a £96 receipt and a capture app extracts the amount incorrectly as £9.60. She checks the image against the accounting entry, corrects the amount and adds the business purpose. She then matches the entry to the bank-feed payment rather than creating a second expense. The legible receipt remains evidence; the checked date, amount and category form part of the digital record. Uploading a photo alone did not complete that process.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Did the evidence reach the accounting record?Check the actual transaction entry rather than the phone gallery or upload status.
Were extracted details checked?Review amount, date, supplier, category and business purpose.
Does the same cost appear in a feed?Match the records and avoid duplicate expenses.

Two more questions you may have

Does photographing a personal purchase make it deductible?

No. The business purpose and any private-use restriction still need checking.

Can I discard an unreadable original after uploading?

Ensure the retained evidence is complete and legible under the applicable record-keeping rules. Replace cropped or unclear images promptly.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Check each image is complete and readable.
  • Verify extracted amount and date.
  • Confirm category and business purpose.
  • Match receipt entries to bank transactions.
  • Resolve duplicates and missing information before updates.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: MTD Software or HMRC Unavailable Near a Deadline: What to Do
excerpt: If MTD software stops working near a deadline, establish what failed and preserve the evidence. A failed login, missing authorisation and an HMRC service outage require different responses. None should be assumed from a general error message.
metaTitle: MTD Software or HMRC Outage: Evidence and Next Steps | TaxSimba
metaDescription: MTD unavailable near a deadline? Identify the failure, keep dated evidence, check official service notices and confirm the submission after recovery.
featuredImageAlt: A taxpayer encounters a neutral laptop service error and records time, error details and next action with adviser.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Help and support - Guidance
GOV.UK — Disagree with a tax decision or penalty: Reasonable excuses
GOV.UK — Issue 148 of agent update

content:
If MTD software stops working near a deadline, establish what failed and preserve the evidence. A failed login, missing authorisation and an HMRC service outage require different responses. None should be assumed from a general error message.

Identify where the problem sits

Check your connection and sign-in details, then the software provider's service information. Check HMRC's published service status through GOV.UK as well. HMRC's October 2026 agent update points users to its consolidated live service issues information.

If your accountant is filing, send the error wording and time of the problem. Avoid sharing passwords or security codes. The accountant should check the filing software and the relevant HMRC authorisation before repeatedly attempting the same submission.

Keep a useful incident record

Record when you first tried, the affected business and period, the error shown, relevant service notices and any support reference. Save screenshots that identify the issue without exposing unnecessary personal data.

For example, evidence that a particular service was unavailable when an otherwise complete submission was attempted is more helpful than a message saying only that the website was slow. Keep a note of when the service became available and what happened next.

Complete the outstanding obligation promptly

An outage does not mean the update has been received. Confirm the actual outcome after service resumes and keep the successful submission evidence. Do not send a duplicate purely because your progress screen is delayed.

Check the rules for the relevant year

HMRC does not apply late-quarterly-update penalty points for 2026/27, but the updates remain required. That treatment does not remove annual return or tax payment obligations. For other penalties, a reasonable-excuse claim depends on the facts and HMRC's rules; an outage is not an automatic guarantee of cancellation.

Contact your accountant early when an issue remains unresolved. TaxSimba can explain what information is needed for work within your engagement and help distinguish an outstanding filing from a display or access problem. Waiting until the last available minute leaves less time to investigate either.

Put it into practice

An error message is not a filing acknowledgement

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

An accountant attempts an update and receives an error at 10:12. The client sends the wording, affected business and period, without passwords or security codes. The accountant checks authorisation, provider status and HMRC's live service information, then records the support reference. After recovery, they check whether the update was accepted before resending. They save the successful acknowledgement and incident timeline; an outage alone does not establish submission or guarantee a penalty appeal outcome.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Connection, access or service outage?Check the relevant provider and HMRC status rather than guessing from a generic error.
What evidence shows the attempted submission?Record time, period, exact error and support references without unnecessary sensitive data.
What happened after recovery?Confirm the actual receipt status and complete any outstanding obligation promptly.

Two more questions you may have

Should I repeatedly resend until the dashboard changes?

First check the submission outcome. A delayed display is different from a failed filing and repeated attempts can confuse the trail.

Does an outage automatically cancel every penalty?

No. Relevant concessions and reasonable-excuse rules depend on the year and facts. Keep evidence and follow the notice's appeal process if needed.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Record the affected business, period and time.
  • Save the exact error and relevant status notice.
  • Check access and authorisation.
  • Retain provider or HMRC support references.
  • Confirm acceptance after recovery and save the acknowledgement.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Dividend Tax: Keep Your 2025/26 Return Separate From 2026/27 Rates
excerpt: Dividend tax rates changed from 6 April 2026. If you are preparing a 2025/26 return now, do not use the newer rates simply because they appear in a current tax calculator.
metaTitle: Dividend Tax: Keep 2025/26 and 2026/27 Separate | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Dividend tax rates differ between 2025/26 and 2026/27. Organise vouchers and investment statements by tax year before checking bands and allowances.
featuredImageAlt: A company shareholder separates dividend vouchers into two tax-year folders while checking different-year documents.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Tax on dividends: Check if you have to pay tax on dividends
GOV.UK — Income Tax rates and allowances for current and previous tax years
GOV.UK — Tax on dividends: Check if you have to pay tax on dividends

content:
Dividend tax rates changed from 6 April 2026. If you are preparing a 2025/26 return now, do not use the newer rates simply because they appear in a current tax calculator.

Which rates belong to which year?

For 2025/26, the dividend ordinary, upper and additional rates are 8.75%, 33.75% and 39.35%. For 2026/27, they are 10.75%, 35.75% and 39.35%. The dividend allowance is £500 in both years. The rate applying to a particular dividend depends on your wider income and available tax bands.

Dividends received between 6 April 2025 and 5 April 2026 belong to the return normally due online by 31 January 2027. Dividends in the following tax year need their own calculation. Do not combine the two years because the same company paid them.

The allowance does not remove the reporting question

Dividends within an ISA are treated differently from dividends outside it. An allowance covering some dividend income also does not mean every taxpayer can ignore dividend information when preparing a return.

If you already complete Self Assessment, give the accountant the full dividend figures. The information is needed to establish the complete income position and apply the allowance correctly.

Gather more than bank transfers

For your own company, provide dividend vouchers and the relevant company records. For investments, obtain tax-year dividend statements from each provider. A transfer labelled drawings is not automatically a lawful dividend, and money paid into your account may need a different explanation.

A useful check before approval

Compare the return's dividend total with your vouchers and investment statements, then check that the calculation uses the year being filed. Where dividends span tax bands, a single headline percentage will not explain the whole result.

TaxSimba can prepare your personal tax return within the agreed scope. Company accounts, dividend legality and director's loan issues may require separate work, so raise those matters before assuming that a personal return package covers them.

Put it into practice

April can divide otherwise similar payments

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A director receives a documented dividend in March 2026 and another in May 2026. She places them in separate tax-year schedules even though both came from the same company. Her accountant checks the applicable year's rates, other income and available bands, rather than copying a current-year calculator into the older return. Investment-provider dividends and ISA holdings are also identified correctly. Company transfers without supporting dividend records are flagged for clarification, not automatically labelled dividends.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Which tax year contains each dividend?Use the actual relevant dates and supporting vouchers or statements.
Which year's rates and allowance apply?Check the calculation for the year being filed rather than today's default calculator.
Does other income use part of the tax bands?Review the full personal income picture before applying a single percentage.

Two more questions you may have

Does the dividend allowance make the income irrelevant to a return?

No. Supply the full relevant dividend information so the annual calculation and reporting can be completed correctly.

Are all company withdrawals dividends?

No. The underlying records and lawful treatment matter. Obtain clarification of salary, loans or other transfers.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Collect dividend vouchers and provider statements.
  • Separate payments by tax year.
  • Identify ISA and non-ISA holdings.
  • List other income affecting tax bands.
  • Check the rates used before approving the return.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Student and Postgraduate Loans on Self Assessment: Avoid Double Counting
excerpt: Self Assessment can include student and postgraduate loan repayments as well as Income Tax. If repayments have already been deducted from your salary, the return must take those deductions into account correctly.
metaTitle: Student Loans on Self Assessment: Avoid Double Counting | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Prepare the right student and postgraduate loan plan details, payroll deductions and repayment-start information for a complete Self Assessment calculation.
featuredImageAlt: A graduate compares payroll loan deductions with loan-plan correspondence and yearly return records.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Tell HMRC about a student or postgraduate loan in your tax return
GOV.UK — Repaying your student loan: How to repay

content:
Self Assessment can include student and postgraduate loan repayments as well as Income Tax. If repayments have already been deducted from your salary, the return must take those deductions into account correctly.

Confirm your loan plan first

Check your Student Loans Company information and the repayment plan that applies to the tax year. Do not choose a plan just because a friend started university at a similar time. Postgraduate loans can apply alongside an undergraduate loan, and the return needs the correct information about both.

Use the rates and thresholds for the year being filed. Different plans have different thresholds, so an estimate made using the wrong plan can give a misleading result. HMRC's return guidance also checks whether repayments were due to start on or before 6 April of that tax year; a newly issued loan does not automatically mean repayments are already due.

Include deductions already made through payroll

Give your accountant your P60 and relevant payslips showing student and postgraduate loan deductions. These amounts are not the same as PAYE Income Tax. Entering payroll deductions in the wrong place can lead to an incorrect remaining liability.

For example, someone employed during the week and self-employed at weekends may already have paid through payroll. The annual calculation can still produce an additional repayment because it takes account of relevant income reported on the return.

Explain direct payments and balance changes

Tell the accountant if you made voluntary payments directly to the Student Loans Company, paid off a balance or received instructions to stop deductions. Do not automatically treat a voluntary payment as an offset against a Self Assessment repayment; the correct treatment needs checking.

If your loan is nearly repaid, compare the return position with the latest loan information and ask how any potential overpayment will be resolved. HMRC and the Student Loans Company have different roles in that process.

Review the calculation as a whole

A larger-than-expected bill is not always extra Income Tax. Ask for the student loan, postgraduate loan, National Insurance and tax components to be explained separately.

TaxSimba can use the plan details and evidence you provide when preparing your return. Supply them early, particularly where employment deductions or a recent repayment make the year-end position less straightforward.

Put it into practice

Payroll deductions must not disappear from the return

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

An employee with weekend self-employment has student loan deductions shown on her P60 and payslips. She gives the accountant the correct plan and repayment-start information, plus any separate postgraduate-loan deductions. The annual calculation can still include further repayment on relevant income, but the payroll amounts need correct treatment. She flags a voluntary direct payment and a near-cleared balance rather than assuming they can be deducted from the return's repayment without checking the rules.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Which plan and repayment start apply?Use Student Loans Company evidence for the tax year.
What did payroll already deduct?Provide student and postgraduate amounts separately from PAYE Income Tax.
Were there direct payments or a cleared balance?Flag them for review instead of treating them as automatic offsets.

Two more questions you may have

Can postgraduate and undergraduate repayments both apply?

Yes, depending on the loans and circumstances. Supply details of both rather than selecting only one.

Is a larger bill necessarily extra Income Tax?

No. Ask for tax, National Insurance, student loan and postgraduate loan components to be shown separately.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Confirm plan types and repayment-start details.
  • Collect P60 and relevant payslips.
  • Separate student and postgraduate payroll deductions.
  • Record direct payments or balance clearance.
  • Review each component of the final calculation.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

excerpt: Your Self Assessment bill may include National Insurance as well as Income Tax. For a 2025/26 sole trader return, use that year's thresholds rather than copying the figures currently displayed for 2026/27.
metaTitle: Self-Employed National Insurance 2025/26: Check the Year | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check Class 4 and Class 2 treatment for your 2025/26 tax return using the correct year's profit figures, employment records and contribution history.
featuredImageAlt: A self-employed worker checks profit records and National Insurance correspondence with accountant, no rate numbers.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Rates and allowances: National Insurance contributions
GOV.UK — National Insurance: introduction: National Insurance classes
GOV.UK — Self-employed National Insurance rates

content:
Your Self Assessment bill may include National Insurance as well as Income Tax. For a 2025/26 sole trader return, use that year's thresholds rather than copying the figures currently displayed for 2026/27.

Class 4 is based on taxable trading profits

For 2025/26, Class 4 is generally 6% on profits over £12,570 up to £50,270, and 2% above £50,270. Other rules can affect the calculation, including age and interaction with employment contributions.

Turnover and profit are different. A trader with £40,000 of sales does not normally calculate Class 4 on the full £40,000 if allowable business costs reduce the taxable profit.

Class 2 does not always mean a separate charge

For 2025/26, qualifying self-employed profits of £6,845 or more generally mean Class 2 is treated as paid to protect the National Insurance record, without a Class 2 payment. Below that level, voluntary Class 2 may be available at £3.50 a week, subject to the relevant conditions.

Do not assume that a voluntary payment is beneficial merely because the option appears. Check your contribution record, existing credits and eligibility before deciding whether to pay. Equally, do not assume that low profit automatically gives you a qualifying year.

Tell the accountant about employment too

If you were employed and self-employed in the same year, provide your P60 and trading records. Employment contributions and self-employed contributions interact under rules that a simple single-income estimate may not capture.

Ordinary residential rental income is not automatically subject to the same National Insurance treatment as a sole trade. Explain what you actually do rather than describing every income source as self-employment.

Check the components before paying

Ask how much of the bill is Income Tax, Class 4 and any voluntary Class 2. Payments on account can also make the amount due differ from the year's liability.

TaxSimba can prepare the return using the relevant year and your full income information. Keep National Insurance questions separate from the monthly fee paid for an MTD accounting service; one is a government liability and the other pays for professional work.

Put it into practice

Profit, not gross sales, starts the Class 4 review

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A trader has £35,000 sales and £9,000 allowable costs before other adjustments. The starting profit figure is £26,000 rather than £35,000 for reviewing profit-based National Insurance. She supplies employment records too, since contributions from more than one source may matter. Her accountant uses 2025/26 thresholds and checks any Class 2 treatment separately. A low-profit year also prompts a contribution-record review rather than an automatic voluntary payment decision.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Are the profit figures tax-adjusted?Separate gross sales, allowable costs and any further adjustments.
Is the calculation using 2025/26 rules?Do not copy current-year Class 2 figures into an earlier return.
Does other employment or age affect the position?Supply the full contribution context and check the NI record where relevant.

Two more questions you may have

Is every Class 2 entry an extra weekly bill?

No. Depending on the year's profit and conditions, Class 2 may be treated as paid. Check the relevant year and eligibility.

Should I always pay voluntary contributions for a low-profit year?

Check the contribution record, existing credits and eligibility first. A voluntary payment is not automatically useful in every case.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Prepare tax-adjusted trading profit.
  • Confirm the tax year used for NI figures.
  • Gather employment contribution records.
  • Check age and other relevant circumstances.
  • Review the NI record before any voluntary-payment decision.

title: Cash Basis or Traditional Accounting: Which Figures Go on Your Return?
excerpt: Your accounting method affects when income and expenses appear in your tax calculation. Cash basis and traditional accounting can produce different figures even when they relate to the same business activity.
metaTitle: Cash Basis vs Traditional Accounting: Timing Matters | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Compare cash basis with traditional accounting, identify unpaid invoices and bills, and check opening adjustments before switching methods.
featuredImageAlt: A consultant compares an unpaid invoice with a later bank receipt on a two-period timeline.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Business records if you're self-employed: Overview
GOV.UK — Cash basis: Overview
GOV.UK — HS222 How to calculate your taxable profits (2026)

content:
Your accounting method affects when income and expenses appear in your tax calculation. Cash basis and traditional accounting can produce different figures even when they relate to the same business activity.

Cash basis follows money received and paid

Under cash basis, income is generally recorded when received and expenses when paid, subject to the tax rules. It became the default accounting method for eligible sole traders and partnerships from 2024/25. Businesses can choose traditional accounting where appropriate, and some are not eligible for cash basis.

An unpaid invoice at 5 April can therefore be treated differently from one that has already been paid. The date you completed the work alone does not establish the cash-basis receipt date.

Traditional accounting follows a different timing approach

Traditional accounting generally recognises income earned and costs incurred for the accounting period, including relevant amounts still unpaid. It can involve debtors, creditors, stock and adjustments that do not appear directly in bank transactions.

For example, an invoice issued in March and paid in May should not simply be moved between years without checking the method. Both methods require a consistent, supportable calculation.

Switching needs a proper reconciliation

Changing method can require adjustments so income and costs are neither omitted nor counted twice. Provide the previous accounts and tax computation before a new accountant prepares the next return. Do not switch merely by selecting a different software option.

Equipment, finance costs, losses and unusual receipts can also require specific treatment. An accounting method is not a general permission to deduct everything leaving the bank.

MTD does not choose the tax treatment for you

Keeping records digitally and sending quarterly summaries are separate from deciding the correct annual taxable profit. The accountant still needs to know the method used and any year-end adjustments required.

Tell TaxSimba which method was used previously and supply outstanding invoices, bills and relevant opening balances. Where you are unsure, provide the last accounts rather than guessing. Establishing the method first makes the return easier to review and reduces the risk of the same transaction appearing in two tax years.

Put it into practice

An unpaid March invoice needs a method check

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A consultant invoices a client in March and receives payment in May. Under cash basis, receipt timing generally drives when income is recorded; traditional accounting uses a different recognition approach. She supplies the invoice, payment date and previous accounts rather than deciding from whichever year gives a preferred bill. If the method changes, the accountant reconciles opening debtors and other balances so that the same income is neither omitted nor counted twice.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Which method was used previously?Locate the prior accounts and return rather than guessing from the software screen.
What remains unpaid at year-end?List invoices, bills and relevant stock or balances.
Is a method change proposed?Prepare the transition reconciliation and confirm eligibility and adjustments first.

Two more questions you may have

Does using a bank feed mean I use cash basis?

No. A record source does not itself establish the accounting method. Confirm the method applied in the tax calculation.

Can I switch just by moving an invoice into next year's folder?

No. Timing and transition rules need consistent treatment supported by the records.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Find the previous accounting method.
  • List unpaid sales invoices and supplier bills.
  • Record stock and relevant opening balances.
  • Keep payment dates and underlying invoices.
  • Confirm any method-change adjustments before filing.

title: Made a Self-Employed Loss? What to Check Before Claiming Relief
excerpt: A business loss does not automatically produce a tax refund. First establish the tax-adjusted loss, then check which reliefs are available and whether a claim would actually benefit you.
metaTitle: Self-Employed Trading Loss: Compare Relief Options | TaxSimba
metaDescription: A trading loss does not guarantee a refund. Establish the tax-adjusted loss, gather earlier returns and compare eligible relief routes and deadlines.
featuredImageAlt: A sole trader brings loss-making business accounts to an adviser to review available options rather than guaranteed refund.

sources.label: GOV.UK — HS227 Losses (2026)

content:
A business loss does not automatically produce a tax refund. First establish the tax-adjusted loss, then check which reliefs are available and whether a claim would actually benefit you.

A cash shortfall is not always a tax loss

Loan repayments, drawings and private spending can reduce the bank balance without being deductible business expenses. Equipment and other costs may need particular treatment. Your accountant should calculate the taxable result before choosing any loss-relief route.

For example, a trader may spend heavily on personal living costs while taking little money from customers. That financial pressure does not establish an allowable trading loss of the same amount.

Different reliefs serve different situations

Depending on the circumstances, a qualifying loss may be carried forward against future profits of the same trade or considered against other income. Special rules can apply to early trading losses, terminal losses and claims involving earlier years.

Conditions, claim deadlines and restrictions vary. Commerciality, the nature of the trade and particular loss-relief limits matter. Foreign trades and claims under the foreign income and gains regime can add further restrictions.

Compare the effect before making a claim

A claim against another year's income might reduce tax, but the result depends on that year's income, allowances and existing reliefs. Using a loss immediately is not necessarily the most useful option. An accountant should compare the available choices rather than assume the largest loss gives the largest refund.

Loss relief is also different from reducing payments on account. The two may interact, but changing future payments does not itself make or establish a loss claim.

Documents your accountant needs

Supply accounts, detailed income and expenses, the trading start date, previous returns, other income and any losses already carried forward. If the business has stopped, give the cessation date and explain outstanding receipts or costs.

TaxSimba can confirm whether the relevant loss calculation and claims are within the agreed service. Ask about additional work involving earlier years before proceeding. A supported claim is more valuable than an advert promising a refund before anyone has examined the records.

Put it into practice

A falling bank balance is not the tax loss

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A trader's bank falls by £8,000, but the outgoings include personal drawings and repayment of loan capital. She separates those items before calculating the trading result. If a qualifying tax loss remains, the accountant compares available relief routes with other income, allowances, carried-forward losses and claim deadlines. An immediate claim against another year is not automatically better than retaining relief for future qualifying profits. The choice needs the full calculation and applicable conditions.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
Is there a supported tax loss?Remove non-deductible private and capital items and check the accounting treatment.
Which relief routes are available?Review conditions, deadlines and prior claims for the trade.
What is the effect across relevant years?Compare available relief rather than assuming the fastest refund is the best outcome.

Two more questions you may have

Does every loss create a repayment?

No. A repayment depends on the available relief, income and tax paid. Some relief may be carried forward instead.

Does reducing payments on account make a loss claim?

No. Advance-payment estimates and formal loss-relief claims are separate processes.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Prepare income, costs and tax adjustments.
  • Record trading start or cessation dates.
  • Collect earlier returns and other-income details.
  • Locate existing loss carry-forward schedules.
  • Compare eligible claims and record their deadlines.

title: Stopped Being Self-Employed? Your Final Return Still Matters
excerpt: Stopping work as a sole trader does not automatically close your Self Assessment obligations. You need to tell HMRC, complete the relevant final return and deal with records or amounts remaining after the business stops.
metaTitle: Stopped Self-Employed? Prepare Your Final Tax Return | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Closing a sole trade still needs HMRC notification and final tax work. Gather cessation dates, unpaid amounts, assets and any remaining MTD obligations.
featuredImageAlt: A closing business owner packs equipment and checks final accounts, cessation date and outstanding return with adviser.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Stop being self-employed
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Add or cease income sources - Guidance

content:
Stopping work as a sole trader does not automatically close your Self Assessment obligations. You need to tell HMRC, complete the relevant final return and deal with records or amounts remaining after the business stops.

Establish the actual cessation date

The date you stopped trading may differ from the date the last customer paid. Give your accountant a timeline covering the final work, invoices, receipts and remaining business assets. The accounting method affects how outstanding amounts are treated.

Use HMRC's process to report that you have stopped being self-employed. Closing a business bank account or cancelling a website does not notify HMRC on your behalf.

Prepare the final taxable result

Include the relevant income and allowable expenses, and review stock, equipment, unpaid amounts and any loss relief. A transfer of the business into a limited company needs particular attention; it is not always a simple closure with no tax consequences.

For example, a trader stopping in February 2026 may still need a 2025/26 return due online by 31 January 2027. Waiting until the next year to tell an accountant can make missing records harder to recover.

MTD businesses have additional closing steps

If the business is within MTD, HMRC's guidance requires the cessation to be recorded and the final relevant quarterly update to be sent. The income still belongs in the annual return for the year it ceased. Other continuing trades or rental businesses may remain within MTD.

Do not simply stop submitting because there were no new customers. A permanent cessation and a quiet trading period are different situations.

Check whether Self Assessment continues

You might still need returns for rent, gains or other income after self-employment ends. Conversely, if no return is needed, ask HMRC to confirm the change rather than ignoring an issued filing notice.

Tell TaxSimba the closure date, what has already been reported and whether other income continues. The accountant can confirm the final-year work, any earlier outstanding returns and the information needed to close the reporting position properly.

Put it into practice

The last job and last payment can be different dates

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A sole trader completes her final job in February 2026 but receives the final invoice payment later. She gives the accountant both dates, unpaid bills, equipment details and the accounting method used. She reports cessation through the official route and prepares the relevant final return. Closing the bank account did not notify HMRC. If she still receives rent, she separately checks continuing Self Assessment or MTD obligations instead of assuming all personal reporting has ended.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
When did the trade actually cease?Prepare a timeline of final work, invoices and receipts.
What remains to be accounted for?Identify unpaid amounts, assets, stock and any final-year loss questions.
Do other reporting duties continue?Check other income, final MTD updates and existing notices to file.

Two more questions you may have

Does cancelling my business website close Self Assessment?

No. Follow HMRC's notification process and complete required final filings.

Can one ceased trade end MTD for my continuing rental business?

Not automatically. Each continuing source and the overall reporting position need checking.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • Record the cessation date and supporting timeline.
  • List unpaid invoices and bills.
  • Identify stock and equipment retained or sold.
  • Notify HMRC through the correct route.
  • Confirm final filings and any continuing personal obligations.
Download the preparation checklist (.txt)

Save completed notes securely. Keep passwords and security codes out of your notes.

title: Content Creator Tax: Sponsorships, Platform Income and Gifted Products
excerpt: Content creation can produce taxable income even when a brand pays with products or services instead of cash. Keep records of the commercial arrangement, not just payments arriving in your bank account.
metaTitle: Content Creator Tax: Cash, Sponsorships and Products | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Prepare creator tax records for advertising, affiliates, sponsorships and non-cash collaborations, with platform reconciliations and private-use details.
featuredImageAlt: A content creator organises sponsorship agreements, platform earnings and gifted-product records beside a camera.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Check if you need to tell HMRC about your income from online platforms
GOV.UK — Selling goods or services on a digital platform

content:
Content creation can produce taxable income even when a brand pays with products or services instead of cash. Keep records of the commercial arrangement, not just payments arriving in your bank account.

Identify the different income streams

Advertising revenue, paid partnerships, affiliate commissions, subscriptions and direct customer payments may all need considering. A product supplied in exchange for promotional work can also have a value for tax purposes.

HMRC's online-platform guidance explains that where gifts or services are received instead of money, their value is relevant. Distinguish a commercial exchange from a genuinely unrelated personal gift; the description used by a brand does not settle the treatment.

Keep evidence behind each collaboration

Save contracts, emails, campaign briefs, invoices, payout statements and details of non-cash items. Note what you agreed to provide, when you received the consideration and how a reasonable value was established.

For example, a hotel stay provided in exchange for promotional posts is not automatically invisible to tax because no cash changed hands. The facts of the arrangement and any genuinely allowable costs need separate review.

Platform payouts can hide deductions

A platform may retain fees before transferring money. Keep the full statement so gross receipts and relevant costs can be reconciled. Avoid counting the bank payout and the underlying platform sale as two separate items of income.

Business and personal use also need distinguishing for phones, equipment, travel and subscriptions. Creating content during a personal holiday does not automatically turn every holiday cost into a business deduction.

Check the reporting route

The trading allowance, Self Assessment registration and MTD eligibility have different tests. If a platform reports information to HMRC, that does not automatically calculate or pay your tax for you.

Tell TaxSimba about all platforms, brand arrangements and other income, including employment. The accountant can confirm the appropriate service and what records are needed. Where foreign payments or complex arrangements are involved, establish the scope before purchase rather than assuming a simple-return package covers every issue.

Put it into practice

A product-for-post arrangement needs a record

Illustrative scenario — not a customer case or personal tax calculation.

A creator agrees promotional work in return for a product rather than cash. She retains the brief, messages, receipt date and evidence supporting its value, then tells the accountant what work was promised. She separately records affiliate payouts and advertising reports. A brand calling something a gift does not settle its tax treatment. Likewise, filming during a personal trip does not make the whole trip deductible: the commercial arrangement and business purpose need separate review.

A decision guide for this situation

What to check and how to act
CheckPractical action
What did each collaboration provide?List cash, products, services and the work agreed in exchange.
Can platform income be reconciled?Keep gross receipts, fees, refunds and payouts without duplication.
Are costs partly personal?Provide purpose and mixed-use facts before claiming travel, clothing or equipment.

Two more questions you may have

Do non-cash collaborations always escape tax?

No. A commercial exchange can have taxable value without a bank payment. Explain the full arrangement.

Does platform reporting calculate my tax?

No. You still need complete records and the correct reporting position across all platforms and income streams.

Your preparation worksheet

Use these prompts to prepare for a conversation with your accountant. No signup is needed to download the plain-text checklist.

  • List all creator income streams.
  • Save collaboration agreements and briefs.
  • Record non-cash consideration and valuation evidence.
  • Reconcile platform statements to payouts.
  • Identify personal and mixed-use spending.
